input:
It is also possible for the heat-transfer result to be carried over to mass transfer by means of the Chilton-Colburn analogy, which essentially sets the mass-transfer factor equal to one half of the friction factor, in the form $j_D = f/2$. The basis of the analogy is the similarity between the momentum and concentration boundary layers: where one and the same surface mechanism governs both transfer processes, the resistance to transfer scales with the resistance to flow, and either coefficient can be used to predict the other. A short numerical check illustrates the size of the prediction. At Re = 20000, taking $f$ = 0.0064 from the friction chart for the surface under consideration, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.0032, and a measured mass-transfer coefficient returning a value near this prediction can be regarded as supporting the analogy for that surface.

An important qualification concerns the friction factor itself. The analogy holds only where the pressure drop arises from skin friction at the surface across which transfer takes place. Where form drag contributes, as in flow across a bluff body or through a fitting that separates the stream, the measured pressure drop includes a component with no counterpart in the transfer at the surface, and a friction factor computed from the total drop will overstate the skin friction. The predicted $j_D$ then stands too high against measurement, and the discrepancy grows with the separated fraction of the flow. For such geometries a better friction chart cannot rescue the analogy, because the defect lies in the quantity fed into it: the skin-friction part of the drag has to be separated first, and in most practical geometries that separation is precisely what is not available, which leaves the analogy resting on surfaces where the flow remains attached

The heat-transfer result carries over to mass transfer through the Chilton-Colburn analogy, which sets the mass-transfer factor equal to half the friction factor, $j_D = f/2$. The analogy rests on the similarity of the momentum and concentration boundary layers: where the same surface mechanism governs both transfer processes, the resistance to transfer scales with the resistance to flow, and either coefficient predicts the other. A short check shows the size of the prediction. At Re = 20000, with $f$ = 0.0064 taken from the friction chart for the surface in question, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.0032, and a measured mass-transfer coefficient that returns a value near the prediction supports the analogy for that surface.

The qualification concerns the friction factor itself. The analogy holds where the pressure drop arises from skin friction at the surface across which transfer occurs. Where form drag contributes, as in flow across a bluff body or through a fitting that separates the stream, the measured pressure drop includes a part with no counterpart in the transfer at the surface, and a friction factor computed from the total drop overstates the skin friction. The predicted $j_D$ then stands high against measurement, and the discrepancy grows with the separated fraction of the flow. For such geometries a better friction chart does not repair the analogy, because the defect lies in the quantity fed into it: the skin-friction part of the drag has to be separated first, and in most practical geometries that separation is exactly what is not available, which leaves the analogy resting on surfaces where the flow stays attached
